pages.description: Replaces the whole list when present.

display_name.description:
Omit to leave unchanged; send `null` to clear it and fall back to the
username.

password.description:
A new password, at least 8 characters.

Setting it ends **every** session this account has, including the one
that sent the request — so the caller has to sign in again.
`sessions_ended` in the response says how many were ended.

oneOf.description:
Owners only. Demoting the last owner is refused with `last_owner`: it
would leave a wiki that requires authentication with nobody able to add
an account to it.

sessions_ended.description:
How many sessions this request ended. Non-zero only when the password
changed, and it includes the session that made the request.

buckets.description: Hours for a day, days for a week or a month, months for a year.

entries.description: Entries overlapping the window at all.

from.description: The window, in UTC. Its edges are local midnights in the offset given.

pages.description: The pages the most time was attached to.

seconds.description:
Time falling inside the window, not the full length of every entry that
touches it: a session spanning midnight is split between the two days.

exists.description:
Whether a page still exists at this slug.

A pin can outlive its page — a file removed or renamed outside Rhizolog
leaves one behind. That is reported rather than cleaned up silently, so
the pin can be removed deliberately.

pinned_at.description: When it was pinned. Pinning an already-pinned page does not change this.

title.description: The pinned page's title, falling back to the slug when no page is there.

limit.description:
How many pins there may be in total, so a client can say why a pin was
refused before it tries.

pins.description:
Oldest pin first. The order is stable: pinning something new appends to
it and re-pinning moves nothing.

analyzer.description:
Which analyzer produced this. Changing any rule's arithmetic, the
tokenizer or the sentence splitter is a version change here, following
`tfidf/v1`.

findings.description: Ordered by start offset, then by rule id.

offsets.description:
What `span` indexes: `page` for one page's body, `document` for a
compiled manuscript.

rules.description:
How many rules were applied.

**Zero and no findings is not a clean page**, it is a wiki that has never
written a rules file, and without this a caller cannot tell the two
apart. `GET /api/prose/rules` answers an empty ruleset rather than a
`404` for the same reason: no rules is a state a wiki is genuinely in,
and it is worth being able to say so.

rules_digest.description:
The stamp of the ruleset these findings came from.

The same string `GET /api/prose/rules` reports. A finding and a ruleset
that disagree on it were produced from different rules, which is
otherwise an invisible way to be confidently wrong about why something
fired.

slug.description: The page asked about. Absent when the body was posted rather than stored.

truncated.description:
Whether the list was cut short.

A `forbid` rule naming one common letter would otherwise return a finding
per occurrence across a whole book. Unlike a compile, a short answer here
is safe to give because it says it is short.

ProseRequest.description: Markdown to check, for an editor that has not saved yet.

content.example: The ferry was late, and being late was all it had ever been.

ReceiptResponse.description:
Why an idea is in the state it is in.

Everything needed to recompute `momentum` is here: the components, the
boundaries they were measured against, and every capture and event that was
counted with a flag saying which window it fell in. A reader should never
have to take the number on trust.

affirmations.description:
Every affirmation and reopening, in decision order. One that fell outside
the window is listed too, flagged as not counted.

captures.description: Every connected capture still readable, oldest first.

computed_at.description: The instant this is an answer about: your `at`, or the server's now.

explanation.description: One sentence per line, each from a fixed template.

missing.description: Connected captures whose files are gone.

ruleset.description: The rules that produced this, and the only thing that changes it.

oneOf.description:
Absent when the evidence is missing. There is then nothing to derive it
from, and inventing one is the thing this feature must never do.

page.description:
The page this idea produced.

It has to exist already and be one you can read. This records what
happened; it does not write a page, and it does not move or copy one.

events.description:
Decision events under `.rhizolog/ideas/events/`. Counted apart from the
threads because they are read by different code and go wrong in
different ways.

times.description:
The time log under `.rhizolog/times/`, which is scanned the same way
and for the same reason.

words.description:
The word log under `.rhizolog/words/`, which is read and replaced rather
than reconciled, and so is not counted like the rest.

RenderRequest.description: Markdown to render, with the context its links need.

content.example:
# Async in Rust

Futures are lazy. See [[notes/rust/pinning]].

oneOf.description:
The slug this content is, or would be, saved at.

It matters only for relative markdown links: `[traits](traits.md)` names
a different page depending on where it is written. Omit it and relative
links resolve from the wiki root. Wikilinks are unaffected — they are
always absolute.

html.description:
The rendered body. Raw HTML in the source is dropped rather than passed
through, and links to pages come back as browsable `/pages/...` URLs.
html.example:
Async in Rust

Futures are lazy. See notes/rust/pinning.

ReplacePage.description: A whole page. Every field is replaced, including the ones left out.

compile.description:
Omitting this puts the page back in the compiled document, since `true`
is what an absent field means.

content.description: Markdown body, without frontmatter. Omitting this empties the page.
content.example:
# Async in Rust

Futures are lazy. See [[notes/rust/pinning]].

contents.description:
Omitting this makes the page an ordinary one again.

**An editor has to send this back whether or not it shows a control for
it.** A `PUT` that leaves it out unmakes a manuscript, which is the same
trap `owner` already sets and the reason that field is filled back in
automatically. This one is not: there is nothing to infer a contents list
from, so the only protection is the client returning what it was given.

due.description: Omitting this clears the due date.

oneOf.description:
Omitting this clears the owner. On a wiki with accounts the server fills
it back in with whoever sent the request, so a `PUT` cannot accidentally
orphan a page you still own.

readers.description: Omitting this clears the reader list.

synopsis.description:
Omitting this clears the synopsis.

**An editor has to send this back whether or not it shows a control for
it**, along with `stage`, `target` and `compile`. See `contents` below
for what a `PUT` that forgets one costs.
synopsis.example: He misses the crossing and decides not to mind.

tags.description: Omitting this clears the page's tags. Use `PATCH` to leave them alone.

title.description:
Send `null` to let the title follow the body's first heading. Sending a
title the server derived is what freezes it — see `title_derived`.

oneOf.description:
Omitting this resets the page to `internal`, as `PUT` does with tags.
Use `PATCH` to leave it alone.

Role.description:
What an account is allowed to do to *the instance*.

Deliberately two values. This is not a permission system: who may read a
given page is decided by that page, and the only instance-wide question is
whether somebody may administer accounts.

count.description:
Calls since the wiki was created. Counts survive restarts; they live in
the durable half of the index, not the rebuildable half.

route.description: The route template, as the OpenAPI document spells it.

rules.description:
Every rule, sorted by `id`, with its options resolved and its defaults
filled in. A wiki that has never written rules answers an empty list
rather than a `404`: no rules is a state a wiki is genuinely in.

rules_digest.description:
Taken over the normalized rules below rather than over the file's bytes,
so a caller can recompute it from this response and check.

score.description: Relevance. Higher is better; comparable only within one result set.

snippet.description:
An excerpt of the body with matched terms wrapped in `<mark>`. This is
here so a caller can judge which hits are worth fetching without
pulling every body.

Only the marks are markup: the text around them is the page body
verbatim and is **not** escaped, so a client rendering this as HTML
would be rendering whatever the page contains.

tags.description: Its tags, so a caller can filter results without fetching each page.

limit.description: The limit that was applied, after clamping.

total.description: Total matches, not the number returned.

content.description:
The section's own text. Only in the `json` format, and only when the
section was `included`.

depth.description: How many contents lists deep this page sits. The root is zero.

length.description: How many bytes they run for. Zero for anything not `included`.

offset.description: Where this section's bytes begin in the document.

ordinal.description:
Where in that list, counting from zero.

The identity of the entry, **not** a position in this manifest. One
contents list may name the same child twice, and a parent reached down
both an excluded path and an included one is walked twice, so its children
appear here twice carrying the same ordinals. Rebuild a contents list by
keying on this, never by counting rows.

parent.description:
The page whose `contents:` list named this entry.

Absent on the root and on a `?style=` preamble, which nothing named.
Always absent or present together with `ordinal`. Present on a gap, a
repeat and a cut chapter as well, where everything else about the page is
absent: these two describe the **entry** rather than the page, and they
are what an entry needs to be moved or corrected.

slug.description:
The slug as the contents list wrote it, so an `invalid` entry can be
found and fixed.

stage.description:
What stage of drafting the page is at, as the author wrote it. Absent on
the same terms as `synopsis`, and the vocabulary is not fixed.

status.description:
One of `included`, `wanted`, `invalid`, `duplicate`, `unreadable`,
`excluded`.

A section keeps its position whatever this says. A manuscript short of a
chapter reports where the chapter was going to be, which is the whole
difference between a gap and an omission.

`wanted` covers a slug with nothing written at it **and** a page this
caller may not read: the two are deliberately indistinguishable.
`duplicate` is a page already emitted earlier, which covers a cycle and
the commoner case that is not one, an appendix listed under two parts.
`excluded` is a page carrying `compile: false`, or anything listed
beneath one: it is out of this document and still in the wiki, still in
the spine, and still drawn in the graph.

subtree.description:
This section's words plus everything emitted beneath it.

Equal to `words` on a leaf. A `duplicate` or `excluded` section
contributes nothing to any ancestor's total, because it contributed
nothing to the document, so this always describes what a reader gets.

synopsis.description:
What the page says it is for, in the author's words.

Plain text and never derived from the prose. Absent when the page says
nothing, and absent for anything that is not `included`, exactly as
`title` is. Render it as characters, never as HTML.
synopsis.example: He misses the crossing and decides not to mind.

target.description:
The page's own `target`, if it names one.

Measured against `subtree` rather than `words`: one rule, recursive. On a
chapter the two numbers are equal; on a part page `words` is the epigraph
and the target means the whole part.

title.description: The page's title. Absent for anything that is not `included`.

words.description:
This section's **own** body, in words. Zero for anything not `included`.

On a part page that is its heading and its epigraph and nothing else,
which is why comparing it against a `target` would draw every part at two
per cent forever. `subtree` is the number that answers that question.

authenticated.description:
Whether this request is signed in. Always true on an open wiki, where
every request is the single user.

authentication_required.description:
Whether this wiki has any accounts at all.

False means it is open: no sign-in is asked for, nothing is refused, and
the dashboard shows no login page. That is the state a fresh wiki is in.

oneOf.description:
The signed-in account. Null on an open wiki, which deliberately has no
account to name, and null when not signed in.

SignalView.description: One term both records carry, and what it was worth.

capture_weight.description: Its weight in this capture, as a component of a unit vector.

contribution.description: `capture_weight * target_weight`. These sum to the similarity.

documents.description:
How many of your captures contain it. The input to its idf, and the
reason a word you use constantly counts for less.

term.description:
A word, or two adjacent words, appearing literally in both. Never a stem
and never a synonym: every signal shown is text you wrote.

Slug.description:
A page's identifier: its path under the wiki root, `/`-separated, without the `.md` extension. `notes/rust/async.md` is `notes/rust/async`.

Slugs must not begin or end with `/`, contain an empty segment, `.`, `..`, a backslash, or any of `< > : " | ? *`. No segment may begin or end with a dot or whitespace, or be a reserved Windows device name such as `CON` or `LPT1` — a wiki written on one operating system stays valid on the other.

A rejected slug comes back as a `400` whose `details.rule` names which of these was broken.

start.description: Byte offset, not a character index and not a position in rendered HTML.

api_usage.description: API calls per route since the wiki was created, busiest first.

last_indexed.description: When the index was last reconciled with the wiki directory.

links.description: Link counts, split by where they point.

wanted_count.description:
Distinct slugs something names and nothing has written.

A wikilink to a page nobody has written, or a `contents:` entry naming a
chapter nobody has written. Both are somewhere the wiki says a page
should be, which is the question this number answers.

SyncCountsView.description: What one scan of one tree found.

failed.description: Files on disk that could not be read, and so are not in the index.

indexed.description: Files read and written to the index.

removed.description: Rows dropped because the file is no longer on disk.

unchanged.description: Files already indexed with a matching mtime and size.

pages.description: How many pages carry this tag.

tag.description: The tag, exactly as pages spell it. Tags are not normalised.

TargetKind.description: Whether a candidate suggests a thread that exists or another loose capture.

name.description: The activity name, which is the group.

running.description: How many of this group's entries are running.

seconds.description: Total tracked, with running entries counted up to now.

totals.description: Every group, every entry, all of it.

TimeId.description:
A time entry's identifier: the UTC instant it was first recorded for, compacted, plus nanoseconds. `20260806T142530-123456789`.

Ids are generated by the server, never chosen by a caller, and they sort chronologically as plain text.

limit.description: The limit that was applied, after clamping.

times.description: Notes are never included here. Newest first unless you say otherwise.

total.description: Total matching entries, not the number returned.

TimePageView.description: A page a time entry is attached to.

exists.description:
Whether a page exists at that slug.

Time can be tracked against a page before it is written, exactly as a
link can point at one. It attaches itself when the page appears, with
nothing to reindex.

title.description: The page's title, or `null` if nothing is written there yet.

name.description: The activity this time was tracked under.

at.description:
The instant everything was computed against. Running entries are
counted up to here.

heatmap.description: When the hours actually go, over the year.

offset_minutes.description: The offset the windows were cut in, as it was applied after clamping.

periods.description: Today, this week, this month and this year, in that order.

TimeSummary.description: A time entry without its note.

has_note.description: Whether the entry carries a note. Fetch the entry itself to read it.

name.description: The activity. Entries are grouped by this, spelled exactly as written.

pages.description: The pages this time is attached to.

running.description:
Whether the timer is still running. Several may run at once, and they
are allowed to overlap.

seconds.description: Elapsed seconds, counting up to now while the entry runs.

size.description: Size of the entry's file on disk, in bytes.

snippet.description:
An excerpt of the note with the matched terms wrapped in `<mark>`,
present only when a `q=` search is what turned this entry up and the
note is what matched it. Absent when the name matched instead — that is
already in `name`.

Only the marks are markup: the text around them is the note verbatim and
is **not** escaped, exactly as in a search hit over pages.
snippet.example: Chased down a lifetime error in the <mark>poll</mark> loop

first_start.description: The earliest entry's start, or `null` for an empty log.

TimeView.description: A time entry and its note.

html.description:
The note rendered to HTML. Present only when `render=true` was asked
for. Wikilinks in a note resolve like anywhere else.

note.description: The note as markdown, without its frontmatter. Usually empty.
note.example: Chased down a lifetime error in the poll loop.

UserView.description:
An account, as the API reports it.

There is no field for the password and there is no `?include=` that adds
one. A hash is not something a client ever needs, and the surest way to keep
it off the wire is for the type that goes on the wire not to have a place to
put it.

display_name.description: The name to show. Falls back to the username.

has_password.description:
Whether this account can be signed in to at all.

False for a file somebody wrote by hand and has not finished. Such an
account still counts towards "this wiki has accounts", so it is worth
being able to see one.

profile.description: Free markdown the account holder wrote about itself.

Username.description:
An account name, which is also the name of the file the account lives in.

Lowercase ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`, starting with a letter or a digit, at most 39 characters. Uppercase is refused rather than folded: Windows filenames are case-insensitive, so `Tim` and `tim` would be one account on one machine and two on another.

A rejected name comes back as a `400` whose `details.rule` names which rule was broken.

total.description:
How many there are. Zero means this wiki is open: no sign-in is asked
for and nothing is refused.

Visibility.description:
Who may read a page.

- `public` — anyone, including callers who have not signed in. Only reaches them when the instance sets `RHIZOLOG_ANONYMOUS_READ`; without that it behaves as `internal`.
- `internal` — any account on this wiki. **This is what an unmarked page means.**
- `restricted` — the accounts in `readers`, plus the owner.
- `private` — the owner alone.

An unrecognised word reads as `private` rather than as the default: a typo in this field must never be the thing that publishes a page.

On a wiki with no accounts this is inert — there is nobody to keep a page from. It is also not a boundary against anyone who can read the wiki directory itself.

referrers.description:
How many pages name it, which is how badly it is wanted.

One page counts once however many ways it asked: linking to a chapter
and also listing it in `contents:` is one page waiting on it.

slug.description: The slug that something names and nothing has written.

actors.description: Busiest tools first, capped at ten.

at.description: The instant the window was computed against.

days.description:
Every local day in the window, including the empty ones, so a client can
draw the chart without filling gaps itself.

offset_minutes.description: The offset the days were cut in, as it was applied after clamping.

pages.description: Busiest pages first, capped at ten.

resolution.description:
Always `observed`, and the field is here to say what that means rather
than to be branched on: **this is not keystroke history**. The watcher
debounces at 500 ms and collapses a burst into one batch, edits made
while the server was down are one observation at the next startup, and
only an API write is genuinely one per save. The counts are right in
every one of those cases; what is lost is resolution in time.

WordSyncView.description:
What reading the word log found.

A different shape from the five trees above, because it is a different
operation. Those are compared file by file and their rows corrected; this one
is read whole and the table over it replaced, so `indexed`, `unchanged` and
`removed` would every one of them be zero for reasons that say nothing.

observations.description:
Observations read back out of `.rhizolog/words/`, which is what the log
held **before** the page scan had a chance to append to it.

read.description:
Whether the log could be read at all.

`false` is a wiki being served with an empty series rather than a wiki
refusing to start. It is also the one case worth acting on: the writing
history is the thing here with no other copy.

skipped.description:
Lines that would not parse. Each costs itself and nothing else, so a
truncated last line after a hard power-off does not lose a year.

pages.description: Distinct pages written to in the window.

tags.name: words
tags.description: The word log: what was written, when, and by which tool. Churn rather than net change, because a rewrite is not the difference between two totals. Working state, so it is never served to a caller who has not signed in.

tags.name: prose
tags.description: prose/v1: holding prose to rules you wrote down. Local, deterministic, and never a model. Every finding quotes the text it fired on and carries the arithmetic behind it.

tags.name: graph
tags.description: Links between pages, tags, and meta-stats

tags.name: times
tags.description: Time tracking: timers, entries, groups, and statistics

tags.description: Idea Inbox: capturing unfinished thoughts, threading them, and deciding about them. Personal working state, so every endpoint answers only for the account making the request and never for an anonymous caller.
